national.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
national.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
national.body:
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.

Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

national.title: Riding wild animals and selling crafts at a prison rodeo
national.summary: Louisiana State Penitentiary hosts a rodeo where incarcerated men risk being stepped on, gored and flipped upside down. But for these volunteer, self-taught cowboys, it's all worth it.
national.body: For most of the year, Kevin "Country" Gildhouse and Travis "Buckethead" Johnson are prison inmates serving a life sentence without parole. But sometimes, they don cowboy hats and spurs for a rodeo dubbed "the wildest show in the South"Through good behavior, around 1,000 incarcerated men at Louisiana State Penitentiary, the largest maximum security prison in the country, earn the right to several privileges, including the option to participate in the Angola Prison Rodeo. Outside the prison walls, the rodeo has elicited charges of exploitation. But inside, the incarcerated men say it's a chance at a fleeting moment of freedom during their life sentences."You're free. You're not in prison. You're just out here competing"Gildhouse remembers being scared to death when he was taken to the Louisiana State Penitentiary nearly two decades ago. "I'm about to go to the place they say I'm gonna die in," he said. Gildhouse grew up in what he described as a broken family. He was in foster care and "bounced through probably about 72 homes throughout my childhood."At 19, he was sentenced to life without parole after he was convicted of killing a cab driver in a botched robbery. To this day, Gildhouse thinks about the man he killed, and while he feels he could never ask for forgiveness from the man's family, he does believe he's been forgiven by God. His life today is very different — especially during the Angola Prison Rodeo, held each year during one weekend in April and on Sundays in October. Gildhouse and other incarcerated me ride wild horses and bulls in front of thousands of spectators."Those few hours that you're out here, you're free. You're not in prison. You're just out here competing," he said. "You're out here with other guys who are gettin' in the mud with you and bleedin' with you. And we love it. We're not forced to do anything here."Inmate John Corley, editor of an award-winning prison magazine called "The Angolite," said the rodeo helps incarcerated men find purpose so they can endure. "You take a guy who has no real chance of getting out and no hope, give him something to do," Corley said. "Make him feel like he's somebody and is accomplishing something, and you've got a whole different guy."Johnson: The man to beatJohnson, the reigning champ, is the man to beat. national.title: This online community of young people is idolizing mass shooters
national.summary: 60 Minutes goes inside a growing, online community of young people who idolize, romanticize and sometimes even seek to emulate mass shooters.
national.body: The True Crime Community, known as the TCC by its members, is a growing online community of young people who idolize and romanticize mass shooters.Allizandra Herberhold is a licensed social worker who's spent two years undercover on social media platforms studying the TCC and its members. Herberhold is what's called a "deradicalizer" and has helped 18 kids leave the TCC. She says most kids age out of the dark interest in violence, but some need extra help."Because I don't speak about them like they're monsters," she said. "I see them as children who are struggling, and they need help."Here are five takeaways from 60 Minutes' report on TCC:TCC is a growing, online subculture Herberhold said most kids inside the TCC are desperate for community, outsiders who are often bullied at school, isolated, and dealing with trouble at home. And like the past mass shooters they idolize, many are battling mental health issues and have a history of self harm. There's also no ideology, according to Katherine Keneally, director of threat prevention at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue. She has been tracking the TCC for the last two years and reports her findings to the FBI and local law enforcement."It's not a social or political change that they're seeking," Keneally said. "It is violence for violence sake and to gain as much popularity and notoriety in the TCC."She said this online subculture is growing not just here in the U.S., but globally. Keneally estimates that there are thousands of TCC members. Their online content ranges from the romantic — with hearts swirling around past shooters faces — to scary, with some posts egging on members to commit violence or announcing their plans to go shoot up a school. Only a fraction go on to commit acts of violence, but Kenneally's team has identified 12 attacks carried out by TCC members in the U.S., just in the last three years. Seven of them were school shootings.One teen who left the TCC, who 60 Minutes is identifying as Vesper, saw the TCC as a place for kids like him to go. He says he planned an attack on his own school in Australia in 2023. His plot was interrupted when a friend he'd confided in alerted the school. Police determined it was a mental health case, so Vesper was brought to a hospital and put on psychiatric hold. national.summary: Nitazenes, a new class of synthetic opioid up to 80 times more potent than fentanyl, are among those being churned out by drug cartels.
national.body: A painkiller addiction after a sports injury led to a promising young athlete's death.Pills Qua Broughton bought over social media were found to contain a nitazene, a new synthetic opioid. Broughton's mom, Frederica Roberson, tried Narcan and CPR, but her son didn't make it. He was 21.Roberson is now warning others about the drug. Nitazenes, which can be up to 80 times more potent than fentanyl, are one of many novel synthetic opioids emerging in the American drug supply. A monthslong 60 Minutes investigation revealed these new opioids are the result of drug cartels tweaking molecules and deadlier chemical concoctions appearing in powders and pills. Cartels come up with new synthetic opioids by making minor tweaks to existing drugs Forensic toxicologist Alex Krotulski, director at the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education outside Philadelphia, was the first person to identify nitazenes in the American drug supply. He looks for new threats by analyzing both seized drugs and blood samples from overdose victims. His lab is on track to identify 50 new drugs this year. Illicit chemists edit existing drugs to come up with new deadly substances, which drug cartels then mix into powders or press into pills. Because the substances are so new, when they first emerge in the U.S. drug supply, they are technically legal. Eventually, regulation catches up, the substance is made illegal, and the drug cartels move on and create other drugs. It's nearly impossible for the Drug Enforcement Administration to keep up with cartels and illicit chemists, who make minor tweaks to the molecular structures of synthetic opioids to create new versions.. "We're not saying, 'Oh, yay, that's gone,'" when a drug is made illegal," Krotulski said. national.title: Army plans to carry out detonation at Iowa plant despite indefinite pause
national.summary: The Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit.
national.body: The U.S. Army says it plans to move forward with the detonation of several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on or by Tuesday, according to a new court filing. It will do so despite a federal court order that paused the detonation plans indefinitely, which the Army said it does not need to follow because of the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.In federal court records filed late Saturday, the Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.On Friday, a federal court suspended the U.S. Army's plan to detonate the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, after community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.The Army originally scheduled two controlled explosions for Friday. The Army then delayed them until Monday before the court stepped in.The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted an emergency motion to pause the demolition after environmental groups filed a lawsuit.Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable, lead-filled explosives in Iowa and what's at riskThe military said on Friday it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible."Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement said.In its filing on Saturday, the government warned that it must conduct the controlled explosion by Tuesday because the temperature is expected to drop below 30 degrees in the next several days. It says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop."A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the court filing says. national.title: COP31 fails to reach major climate deal as talks expose deep divisions
national.summary: Hopes for an agreement on tackling climate change collapsed after a row about mentioning fossil fuels
national.body:
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".

national.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
national.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
national.body:
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

national.title: Lawyer: Father and daughter detained by ICE at Seattle airport were traveling to family baptism
national.summary: Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants.
national.body:
Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Kathy McCormack, Associated Press

Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press

A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

"They've done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said of the father and daughter. "She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it's just heartbreaking."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation's laws."

national.body: A systemwide network issue affecting Delta Air Lines' baggage system that forced teams to manually process bags, resulting in nationwide delays during a busy holiday travel weekend, has been fixed, the airline said Sunday.The airline said in a statement that the automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is now working, several hours after it forced a temporary ground delay program to be issued at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport â Delta Air Lines' mega hub â to manage traffic backups caused by the system outage. The ground delay, which has been lifted, impacted only Delta's flights."Delta apologizes to customers for the delay in their travels today," the airline said. "Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary. For customers facing a canceled flight and don't wish to travel, refunds are being given."Delta warned that while teams are focused on completing the 500 Delta and Delta Connection flights scheduled for Sunday, cancellations would be a last resort if all other options have been exhausted.As of Sunday evening, Delta Air Lines had canceled 202 flights, or 4% of the day's total, departing from the U.S., which is higher than average for the airline. national.title: In their own words: Leaders at UN climate talks discuss why negotiations ended without deal
national.summary: After reviewing a draft of the agreement released by co-host Turkey, a number of countries spoke up during the final meeting Sunday to say they couldn't accept a deal that failed to include wording on fossil fuels.
national.body:
Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press

Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — The words of negotiators and other leaders at the U.N. climate talks illustrate why the meeting failed to reach a final agreement.

Each year the annual meeting seeks to hammer out a document known as a cover decision that gives direction on how countries around the world should fight climate change. But at the meetings in Turkey this time, negotiators could not overcome impasses on whether the final document should mention fossil fuels. The burning of fuels such as coal, oil and gas is what causes global warming.

After reviewing a draft of the agreement released by co-host Turkey, a number of countries spoke up during the final meeting Sunday to say they couldn't accept a deal that failed to include wording on fossil fuels. Others spoke to reporters on the sidelines of the plenary sessions. The co-hosts Turkey and Australia also offered their thoughts.

Below are the views of the players at COP31, in their own words.

"I want to clearly state that the European Union and its member states object to this cover decision in both its iterations, and that we're saying that on behalf of our citizens, our member states, because these decisions go nowhere near the level of action or ambition that are required for us to tackle climate change, it is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel."

"Our responsibility is not to negotiate the minimum threshold, our responsibility is to do what is right. Our responsibility is to protect the planet. ... This is an issue of justice. President, please allow us to explain briefly why Panama cannot support this decision. One, because it repeats previously agreed to commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it (relies) too much upon technologies such as, CCS capture storage of carbon, instead of calling for deep changes. And, three, because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback."

national.title: Natural gas pipeline fire in Alabama lights up night sky
national.summary: Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards above the trees near Ward, Alabama, with smoke billowing into the air.
national.body: A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said.The cause of the fire is under investigation, and customer deliveries were not impacted, Southern Natural Gas Company said in a statement Sunday.Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards above the trees near Ward, with smoke billowing into the air. People said on social media that the fire was visible from miles away across the state line in Mississippi.Southern Natural Gas told CBS News in a statement that it "experienced a natural gas release and fire" on the segment of the pipeline at around 11:30 p.m. CST Saturday. Emergency responders and company personnel secured the area and the blaze was extinguished, the company said. The impacted part of the pipeline was shut down and depressurized.Pleasant Hill Volunteer Fire Department said on social media that its firefighters, along with several other volunteer fire departments, responded to the blaze after midnight to assist Sumter County officials after "a major pipeline explosion that caused a secondary brush fire."The Sumter County Emergency Management Agency did not immediately respond to a voicemail seeking information.Ward is an unincorporated community located near the Mississippi state line. The mayor of nearby York urged residents on Sunday to remain calm and avoid the affected area. Mayor Renee Ward Pringle said in a social media post that the city of York's gas facilities are not believed to be affected.

national.title: Automation system problem at Delta causes flight delays as Americans travel for Thanksgiving
national.summary: Earlier Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued about an hourlong ground stop to some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is Delta's hub and one of the busiest airports in the world.
national.body:
Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Jamie Stengle, Associated Press

Well over half of Delta Air Lines flights were experiencing delays Sunday afternoon following a problem with an automation system during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

The airline said its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they continued to work to restore automation of a system that calculates weight to ensure an aircraft isn't too heavy to fly. Hours later, Delta said that system was once again working, though flights were still not back to normal. About 1,000 of the airline's flights were delayed as of Sunday afternoon.

Earlier Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued about an hourlong ground stop to some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is Delta's hub and one of the busiest airports in the world.

Complying with the weight and balance limits of an aircraft is critical to flight safety, according to an FAA document, and going above the limit can compromise the structural integrity of the aircraft.

The agency said on X that the delays weren't related to FAA air traffic systems.

Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers canceled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights.

The Delta delays come as Americans have been encountering a growing number of problems with technology that are increasingly disrupting their lives.

national.title: Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country
national.summary: The idea of a straight line connecting that "first Thanksgiving" to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth.
national.body:
Samira Mehta, The Conversation Samira Mehta, The Conversation

It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence.

Children learn the story as if it were history — and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn — and, yes, turkeys.

The idea of a straight line connecting that "first Thanksgiving " to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it.

The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts . On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies — and later, states — declared fall holidays of thanksgiving , but did not coordinate with each other.

The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale , who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey's Lady's Book , which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War.

Godey's included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family.

She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian Elizabeth Pleck , Hale began publishing editorials calling for a national Thanksgiving , along with instructions for what the day could look like.

national.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
national.summary: The couple have been together for four years and were engaged in 2025.
national.body:
Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.

A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.

Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.

Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.

In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.

The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.

Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.

The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.

national.title: Appeals court says federal law requiring accommodations for pregnant workers is unconstitutional
national.summary: The appeals court said the act was unconstitutional because a majority of U.S. House members weren't physically present when it was approved as part of a spending package in December 2022.
national.body:
Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press

An appeals court has struck down a federal law that requires workplaces to provide accommodations for pregnant women, saying Congress violated the U.S. Constitution when it passed the law in 2022.

The New Orleans-based 5th Circuit Court of Appeals issued its 9-8 decision on Friday. Advocates of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act said the decision invalidates the law in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, which are covered by the 5th Circuit, and could imperil the law elsewhere.

WATCH: The state of anti-discrimination laws for pregnant workers in America

The appeals court said the act was unconstitutional because a majority of U.S. House members weren't physically present when it was approved as part of a spending package in December 2022. At the time, the House was operating under COVID-era rules that allowed members to vote by proxy.

"The (Quorum) Clause's text, context, original understanding and unbroken historical application all indicate that members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes — as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago and as Congress has done ever since the founding," the court said in its decision. "'Proxy presence' does not count."

A Better Balance, an advocacy group that spearheaded the law's passage, said in a statement Friday that the circuit court ruling would likely be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Inimai Chettiar, the group's president, said the ruling was "legally unsound and short-sighted."

"The 5th Circuit has put the health, livelihoods, and economic security of millions of American women and their families at risk," Chettiar said in a statement.

national.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
national.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
national.body:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.

The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.The vessel had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.A joint investigation was launched with Russia to "uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it," the statement said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. national.title: U.S. Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
national.summary: Environmental groups criticized the government's move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.
national.body:
Jacques Billeaud, Associated Press Jacques Billeaud, Associated Press

The U.S. Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," government lawyers told the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in a filing late Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."

WATCH: Court halts Army detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa

Environmental groups criticized the government's move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.

The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the Army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.

national.title: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeats Rep. Virginia Foxx in House race
national.summary: Chuck Hubbard defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx, CBS News projects, adding to Democrats' sizable majority in the House next year.
national.body: Washington — Chuck Hubbard defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx, CBS News projected 19 days after Election Day, adding to Democrats' sizable majority in the House next year. Hubbard, 64, is a former journalist who took on Foxx for a second time after falling short by almost 10 points in 2024. This cycle, he became the latest Democrat to overcome expectations and flip a House seat.Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, has represented the Tar Heel State in the House since 2005 and is the longest-serving member of the state's congressional delegation. Her loss comes as Democrats saw a slew of wins throughout the country, with key victories delivering them majorities in both chambers in the new Congress. And the dynamic was especially acute in North Carolina, where Democrats flipped several House seats and a Senate seat. Heading into Election Night, the Cook Political Report rated Foxx's seat as likely Republican.Hubbard said Foxx called to concede on Sunday, after a recount had been conducted in the tight race."Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," Hubbard wrote in a post on X. "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."With the victory, Democrats have secured 258 seats in the House, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

national.title: Poland says Russia allegedly twice tried to kill a Ukrainian American rapper
national.summary: Denmark is expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case, perhaps restricting Russian citizens from entering and traveling freely within the EU. Poland said it would support such measures.
national.body:
Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press

WARSAW, Poland (AP) — Denmark has expelled a Russian official after it said it had thwarted an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil. The case took a new twist Sunday when Polish authorities revealed that the same man was allegedly targeted by Moscow's intelligence services last summer in Poland.

Denmark is expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case, perhaps restricting Russian citizens from entering and traveling freely within the EU. Poland said it would support such measures.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Russia's threats were becoming more real, reaching EU soil as the bloc continues supporting Ukraine as Moscow's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark.

The case involves Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and U.S. citizenship, according to Danish media.

The assassination attempt in Denmark was planned for Sept. 25 during a concert north of Copenhagen, according to the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, known by its acronym PET. It said the plot was "planned and initiated by Russian intelligence services."

The plot was thwarted by authorities, the Danish prime minister's office said Friday. PET said two men were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service in operating in Denmark. They were linked to Loyal to Familia, it said, a banned gang known for "extensive, serious and violent criminal activity."

Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying the accusations were unsubstantiated.

national.title: U.S. intelligence chief says Trump's description of Putin as a 'friend' is 'entirely appropriate'
national.summary: Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterized as a betrayal of American values after Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping for rare three-way talks.
national.body:
Jonathan J. Cooper, Associated Press Jonathan J. Cooper, Associated Press

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Sunday it was "entirely appropriate" for President Donald Trump to call Russian leader Vladimir Putin his friend.

WATCH: After calling Putin his friend, Trump 'can't speak to' whether Putin is a friend to America

Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterized as a betrayal of American values after Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping for rare three-way talks. The summit last week in China seemed to be more symbolism than substance, but Trump and his top aides have described it as a historic gathering of the three countries with the largest nuclear arsenals.

Trump raised eyebrows with his warm greeting of Putin and repeated references to him as his "friend," which continued on Saturday, when the Republican president posted an image on Truth Social of him shaking hands with a smiling Putin under the caption, "My Friend."

"In that circle — in that circle of that conversation, using the term 'friend' is entirely appropriate," Clayton said on ABC's "This Week."

He had a similar assessment on CNN's "State of the Union," where he said it was "historic" and "remarkable" for Trump to meet with the presidents of the other leading nuclear powers.

"In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely," Clayton said.

national.title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
national.summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.
national.body:
The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."

The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.

The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.

It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".

The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

national.title: Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats, the largest since 1992
national.summary: The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
national.body:
Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

WATCH: Tennessee Democrat describes how she won a Trump district with almost no ad money

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

national.title: Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back
national.summary: The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer's, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.
national.body:
People in a historically Black corner of Pittsburgh took memory tests, tracked their sleep and blood pressure and shared stories of their past to help scientists unravel risks for Alzheimer's disease.

But they may never get answers. The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer's, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.

Researchers say the move not only wasted more than $8 million in taxpayer money already spent but also is a blow to the hard-earned trust of anxious study participants who won't even learn if their brain tests showed signs of trouble.

WATCH: 'The Price of Exclusion' explores lasting impact of racial inequality in medicine

"The community will look like, 'Oh, they came in here, they took all our stuff, they checked us out. Now they're gonna leave us hanging,'" said Roderick Blair, 70, who had participated in the study for four years.

Trust in U.S. health institutions has long been strained in the Black community, stemming from the nation's long-standing racial health inequities, unequal access to care and bias within the nation's medical system. The legacy of the Tuskegee study, which withheld treatment from Black men who had been infected with syphilis in the 1930s, still casts a shadow.

The Pittsburgh study overcame that mistrust. Getting people involved in the city's Hill and Homewood communities helped get people talking about memory loss, dementia and Alzheimer's and helped challenge misconceptions about it, according to La'Vette Wagner, the Pittsburgh study's field coordinator.

Families who once dismissed memory loss as depression began asking about dementia, and people outside the study called her to ask if family members could join, she said. More than half of Black Americans, or 55%, believe that a significant loss of memory or cognitive abilities is a natural part of aging rather than disease, according to the Alzheimer's Association.

national.summary: Tom Jackson, a former Denver Broncos player and ESPN analyst, has died at 75.
national.body: Former football star and famed broadcaster Tom Jackson has died, his family and ESPN announced Sunday. Jackson rose to prominence as a Denver Broncos player and went on to build a career as a beloved NFL analyst for ESPN, becoming a mainstay of the network's Sunday football programs for three decades, including its "Sunday NFL Countdown" show. He was 75.Jimmy Pitaro, the chairman of ESPN, praised Jackson in a statement released by the network after his death. In it, Pitaro called Jackson "one of the most influential and beloved figures in ESPN's history," who "brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans.""Alongside Chris Berman, he helped make NFL Primetime an iconic part of our football weekends," Pitaro said. "Away from the set, Tom was a trusted colleague, generous mentor and dear friend to many. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him. His legacy at ESPN, throughout the NFL and among the countless fans who admired his incredible work will endure."Jackson's family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wish that his death not be announced until the start of the network's "Sunday NFL Countdown" show by Jackson's longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman."Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom's was frequent and unmistakable," Berman said at the start of the show. "Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. national.title: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
national.summary: South Africa is working to overcome a children's literacy crisis. In one Johannesburg township, a reading club is instilling a love of books in kids — and inspiring them to become authors.
national.body:
Fiona Mogane, 13, contributed the story "Lindani's Modelling Journey" to From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex, a new book of short stories written by kids who are part of the "Read Alex" literacy program in Johannesburg. Participants in weekly classes wrote stories drawing on their own lives. Madalene Cronje for NPR hide caption

JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.

That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where modest brick houses and tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.

But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.

It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex . The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.

South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.

Sandton, widely known as Africa's richest square mile, can be seen in the distance, only a few miles from Alexandra township. Madelene Cronjé/Madelene Cronjé/NPR hide caption

The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.

national.title: French activists demand a tear gas suspension over reported menstrual changes
national.summary: Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints.
national.body:
Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press

PARIS (AP) — French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection.

WATCH: Why French students are leading massive protests across the country

The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons.

Here's what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health.

Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it.

Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches.

national.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
national.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
national.body:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

national.title: As AI detects flaws in computer systems, is it causing more tech outages and disruptions?
national.summary: AI rapidly identifies computer system vulnerabilities and companies are pressured to fix them. Experts say that might lead to unintended consequences, like tech outages.
national.body:
In the span of one week, Microsoft services went down, flights were grounded nationwide, some banks' services briefly stopped working and an internal platform for the National Security Agency went dark.

It left people wondering: Is artificial intelligence the culprit?

In a Fox News interview, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he asked someone in the tech industry what could be causing the outages, and that person believed it's "super intelligence," the Trump administration's preferred term for AI (they're not the same thing).

"That kinda makes sense to me, because I can tell you with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack, no one's out there taking claims for it," Mullin said Nov 17.

WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity

In a separate Nov. 17 Fox Business interview, National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton pointed to flaws that AI detected in a programming language used in systems across the world, and he said fixing them caused unexpected problems.

"The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today," he said.

Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chairman Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said some of the recent outages were "AI-related."

national.title: Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit
national.summary: BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade.
national.body:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries.

The linked robotic explorers — one European, the other Japanese — will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1.7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo.

The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany — 94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away — could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available.

BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade.

NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015.

Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey.

WATCH: Astronauts reflect on living aboard the International Space Station

Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can't wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare "unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time," he noted.

national.title: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
national.summary: Some 200 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual climate negotiations. Countries failed to reach an agreement over fossil fuels - the primary driver of global warming.
national.body:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption

ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.

The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions .

Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.

Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.

Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been formal acknowledgment that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

local.summary: ORCHARD PARK — Greg Rousseau had two sacks, including his team-leading 10th this season, and Buffalo’s defense bailed out the Bills’ sputtering Josh Allen-led offense in a 26-9 win over the injury-depleted division rival Miami Dolphins on Sunday. Allen was limited to a 4-yard touchdown pass to DJ Mo
local.body:
ORCHARD PARK -- Greg Rousseau had two sacks, including his team-leading 10th this season, and Buffalo’s defense bailed out the Bills’ sputtering Josh Allen-led offense in a 26-9 win over the injury-depleted division rival Miami Dolphins on Sunday.

Allen was limited to a 4-yard touchdown pass to DJ Moore with two interceptions in an outing during which Buffalo settled for three field goals on five drives inside Miami’s 20.

James Cook scored on a 1-yard run and had 89 yards rushing to become the NFL’s second player to score a TD and top 75 yards rushing in nine consecutive outings. The only other player to do so was Washington’s Terry Allen, who accomplished the feat in 10 straight games spanning the 1995-96 seasons.

Buffalo improved its AFC-leading record to 9-1 and won its sixth straight, with the past four coming against backup and third-string quarterbacks. Miami’s Kyle McCord was the latest while making his second career start with Malik Willis sidelined by a groin/core injury.

If not for Allen throwing interceptions to end consecutive drives late in the first half, the Bills could have been more dominating.

Rousseau’s two sacks came in the first half during which Buffalo limited Miami to two first downs and 38 yards of offense. The Dolphins finished with 10 first downs and 185 yards, with all of their points scored by kicker Daniel Carlson. He made all three field-goal attempts, including two 52-yarders, after being elevated from the practice squad.

Miami (1-9) has lost four straight since a 28-25 win over the Jets and is off to its worst start to a season since going 0-13 to open 2007.

McCord was 12 of 33 for 102 yards and an interception, and the Dolphins lost their 11th straight trip to Buffalo, including playoffs, in a skid dating to 2017.

local.title: SUNY Brockport employee is released from ICE custody on bond
local.summary: Germán Machado Guillen, a SUNY Brockport employee who was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in mid-October, was released on bond on Nov. 20.
local.body:
Germán Machado Guillen, a SUNY Brockport employee who was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in mid-October, was released on bond Friday afternoon.

Machado Guillen's wife, Maria Velázquez, announced his release over the weekend, saying he had a bond hearing on Nov. 18 and was released two days later, after posting a $25,000 bond.

"We are celebrating Germán's return, but we also want to recognize every person who helped us get here," Velázquez said in a news release. "To those who took the time to care, to act, and to stand with an immigrant family during a frightening and uncertain time: thank you. Your actions made a difference in our lives. We hope our story reminds others that no family should have to face these circumstances alone."

Machado Guillen was taken into custody without warning by ICE agents outside his family home in Batavia in mid-October . Velázquez said that at the time Machado Guillen was arrested, he had a valid Employment Authorization Document to work at SUNY Brockport that expires in 2029. He is also listed on Velázquez’s pending asylum application, as are their two sons.

An ICE spokesperson previously told WXXI News that Machado Guillen's detention was part of a "targeted enforcement action." The agency alleged that the university staffer had overstayed his visa and remained living in the United States illegally, though with a valid work permit, for nearly a decade.

An EAD is issued by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and allows a noncitizen to legally work in the U.S. for a specific period.

The document does not, by itself, establish a person’s immigration status or authorize them to remain in the country — a point ICE previously highlighted in its statement to WXXI News.

"To be clear,” the ICE statement read, “work authorization or a pending application does not confer legal status in the U.S.”

local.body:
The Mental Health Association in Chautauqua County (MHA) November recovery luncheon was not only an opportunity to recognize participants for their accomplishments but to express gratitude to staff and volunteers for their service.

As they have for several years, Bonnie Weber, of Be The Change You Want to See in Jamestown, and her volunteers again prepared and served a delicious dinner at the MHA's Thanksgiving luncheon. Working with her were George Brightman, John Case, Shannon Ramirez, and Bill Schmidt. Jon Bogue offered grace.

Among those receiving certificates for their progress were three participants who completed Strong Foundations, an intense 15-week program, using encouragement, practical tools, and community for single parents to build strong, faith-filled homes.

Weber presented roses not only to the participants but to staff as well, in appreciation of their work and commitment. She also recognized volunteers and community supporters, including John Felton, CEO at the Southern Chautauqua Federal Credit Union.

All are encouraged to mark their calendars now for the MHA's second annual fundraiser at the Frewsburg American Legion on Saturday, February 27. Admission will be free, with basket and gift card raffles, a 50/50 drawing, live music, and food and beverages available for purchase.

The Mental Health Association in Chautauqua County is a peer recovery center offering support groups and individual coaching for people looking to improve their lives, deepen wellness, thrive in recovery, or support those on a recovery path. Peers use their personal stories to help people find recovery in their own lives in their own way.

The Jamestown center is at Door 14 in the rear of the Gateway Center, 31 Water Street. Hours are 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. Monday-Thursday and 9 a.m.-4 p.m. Fridays.

The North County recovery center is open Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays, 9:30 a.m.-4 p.m. in Grace Lutheran Church at 601 Eagle Street in Dunkirk.

local.body:
Every parent wants their children to know how special they are. When better to celebrate than on their birthday.

When my kids started to go to school (in the 1980s), I discovered birthday parties. When it was my daughter's birthday, I did the mom thing and had a party and she invited her friends, and they came. When it was my son's birthday, I tried the same thing, but only one little boy came. It was the boy who was constantly bullied at school. To be his friend meant you were also bullied, but I didn't know any of that then.

Real friendships are built on common bonds and interests, and ultimately, what you get out of a relationship. Who are the friends of children who are different? And when do people really put the feelings of others above themselves?

Today birthday parties can be very creative, and expensive, including taking the party to places outside of the home. It is important to have friends and feel like you belong to a "social" group, but what does it take to make your child feel special these days? And not just that one day, but everyday. I love the "Winnie the Pooh" story of the "unbirthday" celebrations. Then there are 364 days to celebrate with friends instead of just one day. And Eeyore was always included.

But let's go back to the problem of nobody showing up to your party.

Centaur Stride has a program policy to help people make friends and feel special even on their unbirthdays. Friendships and relationships are built on common ground. What does a child with a disability or who is different, neurodivergent or other, have in common with their classmates, cousins or neighborhood kids that is enough to make a bond? One where you have something to talk about, laugh about or just share an experience?

Who doesn't want to go horseback riding? At Centaur Stride, it is definitely not something where social status matters. Our "Friends and Family" program allows a rider to share their lesson with a friend or family member at no additional expense. They can groom a horse together and share ride time. (Instructors must know in advance and all paperwork must be filled out and signed by the participant’s parent.) Would someone say no to a personal invitation like that? local.title: Little Mice by Dunkirk’s Caleb Spell
Seeking a peace, even for modern-day monsters
local.summary: Like many boys growing up in the 1950s and ‘60s, I was fascinated by monsters. My prized possessions were models of classic horror figures. The stories behind them were thrilling — the battle of the giants King Kong and Godzilla, the rag-clad mummy brought back to life from ancient Egypt, and the ha
local.body:
Like many boys growing up in the 1950s and '60s, I was fascinated by monsters. My prized possessions were models of classic horror figures. The stories behind them were thrilling -- the battle of the giants King Kong and Godzilla, the rag-clad mummy brought back to life from ancient Egypt, and the half-fish, half-man Creature who dwelled in the depths of the Black Lagoon.

Of course I outgrew the toys, but my fascination with malformations of nature never disappeared. There are three classic monster figures which, sixty years later, continue to be a source of dark intrigue for me, mainly because of what they tell us about the nature of man.

As a kid, I favored the Wolfman, in part because I loved dogs. If I was to choose my monster self, it would have been that hairy, agile, dog-like beast who howled at the moon. Later, I began to understand the deeper meaning. The wolfman revealed the violent nature that lurks in our subconscious. As a matter of philosophy, it is a reminder of the need for a social contract (laws) because the threat of violence is always there, just beneath the surface. As a matter of psychology, it echoes Freud's theory of the human psyche (the Id). It is, in short, the Beast Within.

During the '80s and '90s, Bram Stoker's original "Dracula" evolved from sheer grotesque barbarism to assume dark, sado-masochistic qualities. The nature of his evil became refined, sexualized, primed for commercial success. Yet, despite sensationalized Dracula sequels, the themes remain intact. It's essentially about the struggle of good versus evil in the context of Christianity and the Holy Cross.

I was teaching a high school AP literature class when I first took on Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," perhaps the most challenging novel I've ever read. This is a story that explores the most complex and disturbing aspects of the human condition.

On a dreary November evening, Victor Frankenstein, the obsessed philosopher/scientist, brings to life his creation -- a human-like creature cobbled together with body parts stolen from the graveyard. Victor has created life from the unliving. In so doing, he assumes the role of God. With that role might have come a responsibility, like that of a father to his son -- a sense of duty to protect and provide for. Instead, Victor Frankenstein is overcome with dread and disgust. He abandons his child.

Frankenstein, the monster, enters the world without a name, without family or guidance. In pursuit of his Maker, he acts out, killing Victor's brother and fleeing into the wilderness. Hiding there, he comes upon the simple home of a happy family led by a blind father. During this time, his only period of peace, he spies on the family and learns of the virtues of life and love. Yet his serenity is short-lived, as the family discovers his wretched appearance and drives him back into the woods. His recourse would be revenge, the burning down of the house of love.

GOWANDA -- The Gowanda High School Thespian Society successfully wrapped up its production of "Clue: High School Edition" earlier this month, completing a three-show run that delivered a high-energy, campy murder mystery to enthusiastic community audiences.

The production transformed the high school auditorium into Boddy Manor through an innovative moveable set conceived by director Ms. K. Merrill, a student teacher who joined longtime producer Mrs. Nobles to lead the show. Building the iconic rooms -- including the Study, Library, Kitchen, Hall, and Billiards Room -- was a collaborative effort involving the entire cast and crew, led by Garry Smith (Head of Construction and Stage Manager) who brought Boddy Manor from just a concept to the reality of Gowanda's auditorium stage. Beyond the ingenious set design, student actors and crew members executed the fast-paced comedy with sharp, clever timing and detailed staging.

Merrill and Nobles guided the production from concept to curtain call, overseeing set construction, character development, and wardrobe design. Senior actors and leads Mallory Berndt (Mrs. White) and Eliza Pound (Ms. Scarlet) stepped up as Costume Co-Captains, helping their fellow cast members build unique costumes, select props, and develop distinct stage personalities.

Following last fall's production of Knock Knock, the directors sought a title tailored to the talents of their ensemble.

“We have returning students who are instinctively funny, so we wanted something a little more grown-up and witty,” said Merrill.

entertainment.title: Molly Meldrum, Australian Music Broadcaster and ‘Countdown’ Host, Dies at 83
entertainment.summary: "Affectionately dubbed 'The Guru,' Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," his family said in a statement.
entertainment.body:
Ian “Molly” Meldrum, the Australian broadcaster, journalist and record producer whose weekly television show made stars of international and local acts alike, died Monday (Nov. 23) at Epworth Hospital in Richmond, Melbourne. He was 83. Explore ABBA Elton John Kylie Minogue See latest videos, charts and news

His family said he died peacefully after a long period of ill health. “Affectionately dubbed ‘The Guru,’ Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music,” they said in a statement. “He shaped not only the sound of a nation but also the dreams of generations who grew up with his voice guiding them.” He is survived by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam. Related Miley Cyrus Marries Maxx Morando in Poolside Ceremony Led by the Flaming Lips' Wayne Coyne Gorillaz Celebrate Mexico's 'Revolutionary Spirit' at Corona Capital, Bring Out Johnny Marr and Trueno BTS, ENHYPEN, BIGBANG & CORTIS Are Big Winners of 2026 MAMA Awards

From 1974 to 1987, Meldrum presented Countdown , the ABC’s Sunday-evening music program, which he co-created with executive producer Michael Shrimpton and producer-director Robbie Weekes. Across 563 episodes, it became appointment viewing for young Australians, and — years before MTV — a showcase that leaned heavily on music video.

The Australian Recording Industry Association said Monday that Meldrum had spent six decades convincing a country raised on British and American records that its own artists could stand alongside the greats.

That reach extended well beyond Australia . ABBA broke there on the strength of clips Meldrum played after their 1974 Eurovision win, scoring six No. 1 singles within two years, with “Fernando” spending 14 weeks atop the chart. “Molly started playing our videos down in Australia and it seemed as though the rest of the world just woke up,” Björn Ulvaeus later said. Madonna landed her first hit single anywhere in April 1984, when “Holiday” aired on the show. Blondie , Cyndi Lauper , Meat Loaf , John Mellencamp and Boz Scaggs all found early Australian audiences the same way.

At home, his endorsement moved records. When Meldrum told viewers to “do yourself a favour” on a Sunday night, ARIA said record stores braced for a hectic Monday. Countdown turned Skyhooks and Sherbet into national names and gave early platforms to AC/DC , INXS , Olivia Newton-John , Divinyls, Icehouse and a teenage Kylie Minogue . Elton John , a longtime friend, has called Meldrum the best thing that ever happened to Australian music.

entertainment.title: Robert Eggers Says He’s “Eager” to Take a Break From Horror Genre After ‘Werwulf’
entertainment.summary: The filmmaker has focused on horror films in recent years, including 'The Witch,' 'The Lighthouse,' 'Nosferatu' and 'Werwulf.'
entertainment.body:
After more than five years of bringing monsters to life on screen, Robert Eggers admits he needs a break from the horror genre.

During a recent Q&A in Mexico, the filmmaker said , “I’m eager not to continue purposely doing Robert Eggers’ House of Horror.”

His comments come ahead of the release of Werwulf on Christmas Day. The film, starring Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp and Willem Dafoe, is set in 14th-century England and follows a town haunted by a beast that threatens a man (Taylor-Johnson) and his family. Related Stories Movies We Now Know What Robert Pattinson Was Doing When the James Bond Casting News Broke Movies Aaron Taylor-Johnson's Monstrous Transformation Teased in Robert Eggers' 'Werwulf' Trailer

“I don’t need to do The Mummy or The Phantom of the Opera . Not to say that I won’t, but I think I need a break,” Eggers added. The director previously tackled witches in 2015’s The Witch , sea creatures in 2019’s The Lighthouse and vampires in 2024’s Nosferatu .

Robert Eggers, who has been praised as a modern icon in horror filmmaking, also addressed the new-wave concept of “elevated horror” within cinema .

“There’s always been horror movies that don’t suck and there’s always been horror movies that are actually probing what darkness is in humankind, and even some of them that have been profound throughout the ages,” he explained. “But what you guys are talking about is something that I think really started with [2014’s] It Follows . Although Ti West was doing this kind of work before then.”

“There’s been a whole lot of filmmakers that have wanted to make personal films, really talented filmmakers with unique voices, and have realized that they can get financing if they do it as a genre film,” the filmmaker continued. “And I think that that’s kind of what this is: people who are telling personal stories with unique voices but are doing it through genre. Not to say that James Wan movies [ Insidious , The Conjuring ] haven’t worked. They’ve been great and also successful. There’s definitely a hunger for horror in general over the past 10 years. But does elevated horror exist? It does. It does because people say so.”

While enjoying his “break” from horror, Eggers is next taking on an adaptation of William Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet for Focus Features .
